title: Sain the barber
hookLine: Sain's aarti offers incense, lamp and ghee, then his whole self (Dhanasri, Sain, ang 695)

lines: AN AARTI ON THE SAME PAGE.
cards: How close do you let a stranger come to your face with a blade? A barber's day is small, careful movements an inch from someone's throat. Trust is the whole job.
Tradition remembers Sain as a barber, and on the same page of the Guru Granth Sahib as Dhanna's grocery list, he left a hymn of worship: an aarti, the lamp ceremony, with incense and flame.
But by the end, what he offers isn't on the tray.

teach.b: Aarti, in Indian worship, is the waving of a lamp before the divine, often with incense and a lamp fed with ghee, clarified butter. Sain's hymn, in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695, opens right there.
In paraphrase: with incense, lamp and ghee I make ready the aarti. And in the next breath: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.
Vaarne jaau, in the Gurmukhi: I give myself over. The tray is set, but the offering is the person holding it. The refrain is pure celebration: joy to the Lord, joy every day to the Sovereign King.
Then Sain looks at the lamp again. The finest lamp, the purest wick, he sings, and turns to the Lord: You are the Immaculate One.
As if the true flame isn't the one in his hand. Then a surprise: he names a teacher. Ramanand, he says, knows the devotion of the Lord, and speaks of the Lord as perfect, supreme bliss.
Ramanand's own hymn comes in a few days. The close: worship the Lord, the supreme bliss, who carries you across the frightening sea.

Tradition tells a story about Sain, retold by the Sikh poet Bhai Gurdas: once he stayed so long with holy people that he missed his duty at the king's court, and the Lord came in his form and served the king in his place.

teach.h: THE WORK AND THE WORSHIP, ONE OFFERING.
teach.b: Whatever you make of the story, it fits the hymn: the barber's work and the barber's worship are one offering.

how: Sain's aarti is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching counts honest work, kirat, as part of a devoted life.

o: a song of mourning sung at the end of a life
worship with a waved lamp, incense and ghee
a barber's tools laid out on a tray

p: knows the devotion of the Lord

s: Sain's hymn offers only incense, lamp and ghee
in the next breath he offers himself: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.
Sain names Ramanand in his hymn
Ramanand knows the devotion of the Lord, he sings.
Sain's hymn is on the same page as Dhanna's
both are in Raag Dhanasri on Ang 695.

games.q: in the story people tell, Sain is with holy people and it's time for his duty at the king's court. what happens?
o: he runs to the palace and apologizes.
he stays, and the Lord serves the king in his form.
he quits his job to become a wandering monk.
games.why: in the story Bhai Gurdas retells, the Lord came in Sain's form and served the king, so the barber's work and worship became one offering.

practice: Picture what your hands will do today, emails, meals, a shift, a diaper, a classroom, and see its tools the way Sain had scissors and comb.
Quietly offer the work itself, done carefully, as your aarti, whether you call it that or not. If you pray, let Waheguru ride each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Aarti. The lamp ceremony of worship, incense and ghee on the tray, until Sain turns himself into the offering: I am a sacrifice to the Lord.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the lamp ceremony of worship; Sain's hymn makes himself the offering (Ang 695).

carryVoice: Your line: the barber's aarti. Scissors and comb belong on the tray too. That's day seven hundred eighty-three.
